Title: â€˜Not Normalâ€™: Dems Say Their Party Members â€˜Have Begun To Speak Like Professorsâ€™
Text: A growing number of Democrats are arguing that members of their party need to reconsider their use of certain left-wing words and phrases if they want to better connect with voters they lost in the 2024 election cycle, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday. Some members of the Democratic Party are raising concerns that many of their candidates have become too reliant on using elite-sounding phrases, which they claim is a type of language that could isolate working-class voters, according to the Washington Post. The article cites examples of left-wing words and phrases often used by Democrats, such as â€œoligarchs,â€ â€œequity,â€ â€œjustice-involved populationsâ€ and â€œintersectionality.â€ â€œSome words are just too Ivy League-tested terms,â€ Democratic Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego told the Washington Post. â€œIâ€™m going to piss some people off by saying this, but â€˜social equityâ€™ â€” why do we say that? Why donâ€™t we say, â€˜We want you to have an even chanceâ€™?â€ Meanwhile, Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear told the Washington Post he believes that Democrats using certain left-wing words can result in them sounding like they are â€œnot normal.â€ â€œI believe that, over time, and probably for well-meaning reasons, Democrats have begun to speak like professors and started using advocacy-speak that was meant to reduce stigma, but also removed the meaning and emotion behind words,â€ Beshear told the outlet, citing examples such as referring to addiction as â€œsubstance abuse disorder.â€ â€œIt makes Democrats or candidates using this speech sounding like theyâ€™re not normal,â€ Beshear added. â€œIt sounds simple, but what the Democratic Party needs to do is be normal and sound normal.â€ The Washington Postâ€™s report comes amid a growing number of reports that the Democratic Party is attempting to develop a new messaging strategy to regain voters they lost in the 2024 presidential and Congressional elections. The party has also faced a slew of recent surveys showing poor approval ratings among voters. Similarly, Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chair Ken Martin said in February that Americans now view the Republican Party as the party of the working class and see the Democratic Party as the â€œparty of the elites.â€ â€œHonestly, Democrats trip over themselves in an attempt to say exactly the right thing,â€ Allison Prasch, who teaches rhetoric, politics and culture at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, told the Washington Post. â€œRepublicans maybe arenâ€™t so concerned about saying exactly the right thing, so it may appear more authentic to some voters.â€ â€œRepublicans have a willingness to paint with very broad brushstrokes, where Democrats are more concerned with articulating multiple perspectives,â€ Prasch added. â€œAnd, because of that, they can be hampered by the words and phrases they utilize.â€ Earlier in May, Democratic strategist James Carville said he believes that Democrats need to stop using a spate of left-wing words and phrases he deemed as ineffective or isolating to voters, citing language such as â€œoligarchy,â€ â€œequityâ€ and â€œgenerational change.â€ Carville added that he thinks some left-wing words used by Democrats are often â€œjust not helpful.â€ â€œWeâ€™re going to have limited time to make our case. When we have whatever limited time we have, and weâ€™re fighting back at all this, I think we should be very careful â€¦ So when you hear your elected representatives and you hear Democrats or you hear sane people using words that are not the right word, let them know that that kind of language is not helpful,â€ Carville said at the time. â€œIt doesnâ€™t mean youâ€™re a bad person â€” itâ€™s just not helpful.â€ Relatedly, Rahm Emanuel, a former Obama White House chief of staff whose name has recently been floated as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, claimed in a Wall Street Journal interview published Monday that the Democratic Party brand is â€œweak and woke.â€ All content created by the Daily Caller News Foundation, an independent and nonpartisan newswire service, is available without charge to any legitimate news publisher that can provide a large audience. Title: New York Lawmakers Pass Assisted Suicide Bill, Send to Governorâ€™s Desk
Text: New York state Senate Democrats passed a controversial bill on Monday that would legalize physician-assisted suicide for terminally ill people. The bill is now sitting on Gov. Kathy Hochulâ€™s (D) desk â€” the governor has not indicated whether she will sign the bill, but her office said she will â€œreview the legislation,â€ according to the New York Post.  The bill, called the â€œMedical Aid in Dyingâ€ bill by supporters, would allow physicians to prescribe lethal drugs to people with a prognosis of six months or less to live. The measure passed 35 to 27, with six Democrats â€” Senators April Baskin, Siela Bynoe, Cordelle Cleare, Monica Martinez, Roxanne Persaud, and Sam Sutton â€“ breaking with their party to vote against it.  Critics of the bill warn it lacks important safeguards, such as a mandatory waiting period, a clear chain of custody for the lethal drugs, mandatory in-person appointments with doctors, and disclosure confirming the individual followed through in taking the drugs to end their own lives, according to the report. The bill only requires terminally ill individuals to receive approval from two doctors and a sign-off from two independent witnesses before receiving the lethal drugs.  The New York Alliance Against Assisted Suicide released a statement following the vote encouraging Hochul to veto the bill.  â€œThe Governor still has the opportunity to uphold New Yorkâ€™s commitment to suicide prevention, protect vulnerable communities, and affirm that every lifeâ€”regardless of disability, age, or diagnosisâ€”is worthy of care, dignity, and protection,â€ the group said.  Dennis Poust, executive director of the New York State Catholic Conference, released a statement warning that â€œthis is only the beginning.â€  â€œFor the first time in its history, New York is on the verge of authorizing doctors to help their patients commit suicide,â€ Poust said. â€œMake no mistake â€“ this is only the beginning, and the only person standing between New York and the assisted suicide nightmare unfolding in Canada is Governor Hochul.â€  Lawmakers passed the bill after the American Medical Association (AMA) reaffirmed its opposition to physician-assisted suicide.  If Hochul signs the bill, New York will become the 12th state, plus Washington, D.C., to legalize assisted suicide. Delaware became the 11th state to legalize the practice last month. Title: FACT FOCUS: A Craigslist ad is not proof of paid protesters in LA. It was posted as a prank
Text: As demonstrations in Los Angeles over immigration raids unfolded in recent days, social media users falsely cited a Craigslist ad as evidence that protesters had been paid to participate. â€œWe are forming a select team of THE TOUGHEST dudes in the area,â€ the ad, which is no longer live, read. â€œThis unit will be activated only when the situation demands it â€” BUT YOU GET PAID EVERY WEEK NO MATTER WHAT. high-pressure, high-risk, no room for hesitation. We need individuals who do not break, panic, or fold under stress and are basically kickass dudes.â€ It offered $6,500-$12,500 in compensation per week. But the ad was a prank, it is not related to the Los Angeles protests. Hereâ€™s a closer look at the facts. CLAIM: A Craigslist ad seeking â€œthe toughest badasses in the cityâ€ is proof that Los Angeles demonstrations over immigration raids are made up of paid protesters. THE FACTS: This is false. The ad, which appeared in Craigslistâ€™s Los Angeles section for general labor jobs, was bait for a prank show and had nothing to do with the protests in Los Angeles, the adâ€™s creator told The Associated Press. It was posted on Thursday, the day before the protests began. In a livestreamed episode on Friday, the showâ€™s hosts called and spoke with people who responded to the ad. â€œI literally had no idea it was ever going to be connected to the riots. It was a really weird coincidence,â€ said Joey LaFleur, who posted the ad on Craigslist.  The ad was developed as part of a new prank show called â€œGoofcon1,â€ said LaFleur, who hosts the podcast with Logan Quiroz. On their show Friday, the day protests began, they spoke live on the phone with people who responded during Goofcon1â€™s third episode. LaFleur noted during the episode that he also posted a more â€œmilitaristicâ€ version of the ad in Craigslistâ€™s Austin section, but didnâ€™t get many responses. Screenshots of the ad were used in social media posts on multiple platforms, cited as proof that those involved in the Los Angeles protests had been paid. The posts gained tens of thousands of likes, shares, and views. â€œCALIFORNIA RIOT IS A FUNDED OPERATION,â€ reads one X post sharing the ad. â€œDestabilizing the Trump administration and the United States in general is the goal. Then, they receive billions of federal funding to â€˜fixâ€™ the damage and pocket the money.â€ A TikTok video sharing the ad viewed approximately 14,100 times called protesters â€œpaid agitatorsâ€ who are turning â€œwhat was initially a peaceful protest of just marching into a full-blown riot.â€ Others pointed to the ad as evidence that the protests â€œarenâ€™t organicâ€ or have been faked by Democrats. After screenshots of the ad spread on social media, LaFleur posted about the confusion on his Instagram story multiple times. â€œAccidentally goofed the entire nation on the latest @goofcon1,â€ one post reads. In another, he muses: â€œI donâ€™t really know what to do with any of this. I guess get on Newsmax, or something. If I get on Newsmax, that could be funny.â€ False claims about paid protesters regularly spread around demonstrations, especially those that attract national or international attention. Similar false claims spread widely in 2020 during demonstrations over George Floydâ€™s death at the hands of Minneapolis police. ___ Find AP Fact Checks here: https://apnews.com/APFactCheck.

Title: How Charlie Rangel Defied His Party to Save New York From the Reactionary Right
Text: The late congressmanâ€™s upending of New York politics by choosing progressivism over partisanship offers a lesson for today. Charlie Rangel in Harlem in 1970. Former US representative Charles Rangelâ€™s death at age 94 has inspired long obituaries recalling the legacy of the Harlem Democrat, who served 46 years in the US House, cofounded the Congressional Black Caucus, chaired the powerful Ways and Means Committee, shaped the character of the Congress and was censured by it, earned a Purple Heart for his wounds and the Bronze Star with Valor for his bravery during the Korean War, and later emerged as one of the boldest critics of George W. Bushâ€™s Iraq War. Yet one of the most remarkable maneuvers of Rangelâ€™s long political career has gone mostly unmentionedâ€”perhaps because it does not fit easily within the partisan narratives of American politics. In 1969, with Richard Nixon, a Republican determined to exploit unrest and racial division for partisan advantage, in the White House, and conservative Democrats (seemingly influenced by the presidential bids of Alabama segregationist George Wallace) scheming to pull the party to the right, New York was at the center of the fight for the soul of American politics. Rangel, then a young state legislator who had caught the attention of Democratic leaders that year with an audacious if ultimately unsuccessful primary bid for City Council president, suddenly found himself in a position to push back against the politics of reaction in New York. But he could not do so from within his own Democratic Party. The cityâ€™s 1969 mayoral race produced June primary results that suggested New York was veering to the right. John Lindsay, the liberal Republican incumbent mayor who was up for reelection, was defeated in the GOP primary by state Senator John Marchi, a conservative with ties to the Nixon White House. On the Democratic side, the most right-wing candidate, City Comptroller Mario Procaccino, beat more liberal contendersâ€”including former mayor Robert Wagner Jr., Bronx Borough President Herman Badillo and novelist Norman Mailerâ€”with a campaign that attacked â€œlimousine liberalsâ€ (a term he is actually credited with inventing), exploited opposition to desegregation and open housing, and employed â€œlaw-and-orderâ€ dog whistles to bring the worst of national politics to the nationâ€™s largest city. Alabamaâ€™s Wallace hailed the results from the Big Apple, claiming that Procaccino and Marchi engaged in the same sort of campaigning that he perpetuated in the South, â€œexcept that they had New York accents.â€ After his primary defeat, Lindsay decided to keep running as an advocate for civil rights, a proponent of anti-poverty programs, a foe of the Vietnam War, and the only prominent progressive in the field. He had the endorsement and ballot line of New Yorkâ€™s small Liberal Party, and he hoped to swing enough progressive Black, Puerto Rican, and Jewish voters away from the Democratic line to prevail. But in an overwhelmingly Democratic city, and with two Republicans potentially splitting the vote, Procaccino was the clear front-runner. Pundits said he could win simply by keeping most of his partyâ€™s multiracial, multiethnic voter base on his side. But Charlie Rangel was not about to side with Mario Procaccino. Shortly after the primary election, the Harlem legislator upended the cityâ€™s political calculus by becoming the first prominent Black Democratic elected official to support Lindsayâ€™s reelection bid. Forty-six years later, New York faces another definitive mayoral election, which once again pits rival Democratic factions against each other. These are different political times. But endorsements continue to influence the outcome of municipal races. And what Rangel did in July 1969 offers a reminder of the outsized role that political prescience, and courage, can play in city politics. Rangelâ€™s decision to break with party orthodoxyâ€”at a point when other prominent Democrats were wrestling with whether to back Lindsayâ€”was such a big deal that New Yorkâ€™s media corps packed the press conference where he and the mayor shook up urban politics. â€œIn New York City, the Democratic Party has traditionally represented a symbol of hope that one day the benefits promised in our constitution would be extended to include the poor, the persecuted and the denied,â€ said Rangel, who argued that Procaccino had betrayed the partyâ€™s commitment to address the needs of those â€œentangled in the barbed-wire of prejudice, racial and economic discrimination.â€ â€œToday,â€ he warned, â€œa voter can no longer depend on the party label to determine the philosophy of the partyâ€™s candidate. I have taken a long hard look at [the issues and the contenders], and in good conscience I must reject my partyâ€™s candidate for mayor of the city of New York. In doing this, I break from my family and communityâ€™s tradition. But I believe that a united party is far less important than a united cityâ€”because if our cities are torn apart then, indeed, what is there to hope for?â€ A hush fell over the press room as Rangel continued. â€œWhile, politically, it may be wise for me to sit this election out, I believe my higher duty is to attempt to bring our people together once again,â€ he said. â€œI believe that our present mayor, Mayor John Lindsay, is the best person to do that job.â€¦ I intend to work very hard toward his reelection and Iâ€™m convinced that, with his efforts and the efforts of other people in the city of New York, we will have the type of voter registration drive that would make it possible for all future candidates of the Democratic Party to understand that they cannot afford to move to fall away from the traditions of our great party.â€ Lindsay welcomed the endorsement as â€œa very meaningful moveâ€ that would help forge â€œa coalition, an independent coalition, that can move our city forward in a joining of all persons of progressive spirit.â€ After Rangelâ€™s announcement, that coalition rapidly expanded. The powerful New Democratic Coalition, a group tied to the Democratic reform movements that had gained traction in critical Jewish, Black, and Puerto Rican precincts, endorsed Lindsayâ€”in a move that The New York Times wrote, â€œofficially puts the cityâ€™s most liberal citizens behind the Mayor.â€ Five days later, US Representative Shirley Chisholm, the Democratic National Committee member from New York who three years later would become the first Black woman to bid for the partyâ€™s presidential nod, endorsed Lindsay. â€œThe situation in New York City is so critical and so important that none of us should let partisan politics stand in our way,â€ declared Chisholm. â€œOur times and our cities do not allow this kind of thing.â€ CHRIS LEHMANN BOOKS & THE ARTS / MICHAEL EBY   The momentum grew, as prominent white liberalsâ€”such as Paul Oâ€™Dwyer, the New Democratic Coalition leader and 1968 Democratic nominee for the US Senateâ€”joined Rangel and Chisholm in backing Lindsay. By late October, the Times was reporting, â€œMost political activity in central Harlem involves Lindsayâ€™s campaign.â€ That proved to be vital. On election day, the mayor won reelection, with strong support from Harlem and other Black neighborhoods for a Republican who, the Times observed, â€œhad earned the confidence of the disadvantaged and minority groups of the city.â€ Rangelâ€™s early decision to break with his own party had proven to be the â€œvery meaningful moveâ€ Lindsay predicted. The mayorâ€™s second term would be marred by controversy, and bitter disputes with Nixon and the GOPâ€”culminating in Lindsayâ€™s 1971 decision to register as a Democrat. Rangel would, in 1970, defeat US Representative Adam Clayton Powell Jr., in a headline-grabbing result that followed a campaign which saw the mayor appear on 125th Street and Seventh Avenue to hail Rangel as candidate who was â€œyoung, energetic and committed to social changeâ€ and who Lindsay predicted would make â€œa vigorous, active congressman.â€ John Nichols is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation. He has written, cowritten, or edited over a dozen books on topics ranging from histories of American socialism and the Democratic Party to analyses of US and global media systems. His latest, cowritten with Senator Bernie Sanders, is the New York Times bestseller It's OK to Be Angry About Capitalism.
